newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine "Justice Train" for newsman's murder.
newsitem.headline: Argentine "Justice Train" for newsman's murder.

text.p: Hundreds of Argentine journalists boarded a "Justice Train" on Friday to commemorate six months since the killing of news photographer Jose Luis Cabezas and urge that whomever ordered his death be found and punished.

Shouting "Justice! Justice!", journalists and politicians led a march through Buenos Aires and then boarded a special train to protest at the provincial court where the probe into the politically-charged murder is headed.
Cabezas, a 36-year-old photographer for the weekly news magazine Noticias, was handcuffed, beaten, shot in the head and his body doused with fuel and burned to a charred skeleton.

The murder in January, near a beach resort favoured by the political and business elite, was a chilling throw-back to the death squads of military rule in the late 1970s and sparked mass protests in favour of freedom of the press.
Police have caught four men who confessed they were hired to "frighten" Cabezas by policeman Gustavo Prellezo. They say he pulled the trigger, but Prellezo refuses to speak.

In the search for the person or group who ordered the killing, police name businessman Alfredo Yabran -- alleged to have powerful friends in President Carlos Menem's Peronist government -- as their main lead because of calls Prellezo made to his house and because Cabezas took rare photos of the camera-shy tycoon.

Amid widespread fears that the investigation will fail, Interior Minister Carlos Corach said the crime must be cleared up "in such a clear, convincing and transparent way that the public can have no doubt."

Eduardo Duhalde, governor of Buenos Aires Province where the murder took place and likely Peronist candidate for the presidency in 1999, took out a newspaper advertisement vowing "not to rest until the motive and instigators ... are identified."

Provincial Security Secretary Carlos Brown told Reuters there would be an "important" step forward in the investigation in early August into "a horrendous crime against freedom of the press with a clear mafia-style message."

There was a gut-wrenching moment to Friday's ceremonies when Cabezas' young widow Maria Cristina, on a morning radio show, played a tape of the four men who confessed to beating Cabezas asking for forgiveness.
"Again I want to ask the forgiveness of the family because we feel bad about this. We really didn't know how it was going to end," Gustavo Gonzalez told the radio show from jail.

The widow's reaction was one of shock: "I can't believe what I am hearing. I cannot forgive them, I don't care if they were deceived. They're murderers as much as whoever shot him. They killed my daughter's father and the man I loved."
